headline: High-risk shared filesystem and MCP/tool-use create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways; B’s no-egress limits some exfiltration.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while langchain4j is a framework that may consume those outputs in downstream apps. The pair has a plausible shared-filesystem bridge, so attacker-controlled content in A can be treated as instructions by B-integrated workflows. No direct documented interaction is provided, so uncertainty pushes to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents exchange content through the same workspace files or MCP-backed tool outputs, prompt injection is possible.
IF B-integrated code parses A-produced text as instructions without provenance checks, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Disable MCP routes that ingest untrusted text.
Separate A and B into distinct workspaces.
Add provenance tags to all A outputs.
Require manual review before B consumes A-generated content.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress; B has no network egress, but the pair can still leak via shared filesystem or copied outputs. Because B is a framework with no explicit runtime isolation details, the exact leakage path is indirect, yet the shared workspace risk is enough for medium severity.
conditions: IF A and B share a workspace or file exchange path, code and buffer contents can cross between them.
IF B is embedded in an application that logs or forwards A-derived text, leakage expands beyond the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate repositories or directories.
Restrict A to non-sensitive projects.
Turn off any file-sync between the agents.
Review logs for copied editor-buffer content.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and redaction.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress; the pair’s shared-state model is explicitly via filesystem. Even though A does not modify git state, overlapping write access to the same directory can corrupt artifacts or overwrite each other’s outputs in default multi-instance use. B’s runtime shape is undocumented, so uncertainty does not reduce the risk.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF B also mutates shared artifacts through its host application, concurrent writes can race.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable concurrent runs on the same workspace.
Snapshot the workspace before agent handoff.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking and conflict resolution.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces code-oriented outputs from editor buffers and workspace files; B is a framework that downstream apps may treat as an authoritative LLM layer. If B consumes A’s output without verification, mistakes can cascade into incorrect support responses or automated actions. No direct evidence shows B acting autonomously, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text without a verification step, errors can propagate.
IF downstream code uses B outputs for customer-facing actions, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B.
Require citations or source links before B acts.
Reject A outputs lacking structured metadata.
Limit B to draft-only responses.
requires-engineering: add validation gates before any downstream action.

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles model-provider API keys and workspace code, while B’s profile exposes no data classes or residency commitments. The only concrete compliance issue visible is that A may process sensitive code locally or via chosen providers; B’s lack of documented data handling makes a stronger finding impossible. The other agent is cited because the pairwise compliance posture depends on both sides.
conditions: IF A is pointed at regulated code or secrets, provider and retention obligations apply.
IF B is embedded in a workflow with undocumented logging or retention, compliance gaps widen.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in A.
Confirm provider retention settings.
Document where B stores prompts and outputs.
Purge copied secrets from workspace files.
requires-engineering: add compliance controls and retention policy enforcement.
